stories.headline: Tom Brady tops list of athletes who became owners
stories.summary: The legendary quarterback is a member of an exclusive list of athletes that includes LeBron James, Serena Williams and Wayne Gretzky.
stories.body:
Tom Brady is getting (back) into the ownership game.

On Friday, sources confirmed to ESPN and NFL Network that the former superstar quarterback had bought shares in the English soccer giants Chelsea. Brady's purchasing of Chelsea shares comes after he departed the ownership group of another English club, EFL Championship side Birmingham City, earlier in the month after originally becoming a minority owner with a 3.3% stake.

Brady's latest interest isn't his only foray into the world of ownership -- he also owns a 5% minority stake in the Las Vegas Raiders, purchased in 2024, and he also has a stake in the Las Vegas Aces.

The NFL legend is far from the first athlete, active or former, to enter the ownership sphere. Here are other athletes who are now team owners:

Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, Atlético Madrid

In October 26 news broke that the star Oklahoma City Thunder guard would be joining the club as an investor.

"I am excited to officially join the group of shareholders of Atlético de Madrid," Gilgeous-Alexander said in the club's post. "This is a club with a long history at the top of European football, and I am grateful for the opportunity to be part of its future."

Jason Kidd -- Everton

In April 2025, English Premier League club Everton announced that then-Dallas Mavericks coach Jason Kidd would be adding a different title to his résumé: ownership group member. The news came after Kidd joined Roundhouse Capital Holdings, which is part of the Friedkin Group -- the U.S. firm that completed its takeover of Everton's ownership the previous December.

Vince Carter, Tracy McGrady, Jozy Altidore -- Buffalo Bills

In December 2024, the Bills announced Carter, McGrady and Altidore were among 10 limited partners the team was adding to its ownership group. Both McGrady (New York Knicks) and Altidore (New York Red Bulls) played for New York-area teams, while Carter spent time with the Brooklyn Nets (who were known as the New Jersey Nets at the time) and was McGrady's teammate on the Toronto Raptors (who are closer to Buffalo than NYC-based teams).

Tom Brady -- Las Vegas Aces, Las Vegas Raiders, Chelsea

The Las Vegas Aces, the reigning WNBA champions, have added to their championship credentials. Seven-time Super Bowl champion Tom Brady acquired a minority stake in the team whose majority owner is Las Vegas Raiders owner Mark Davis.

"I have always been a huge fan of women's sports, and I admire the work that the Aces' players, staff, and the WNBA continue to do to grow the sport and empower future generations of athletes," Brady said in a statement. "To be able to contribute in any way to that mission as a member of the Aces organization is an incredible honor."

Brady attended an Aces game in May 2022 and sent gifts to star Kelsey Plum. Plum and other Aces players were excited to have Brady as part of the team.

He also added the Las Vegas Raiders to his resume after his purchase of minority stake in the franchise was approved by NFL teams owners on Tuesday. The deal was agreed on in May 2023, but it took owners 17 months to give their approval over concerns he was receiving too much of a discount from majority owner Mark Davis.

Brady was also a minority owner of Birmingham City, a club in English soccer's second-tier Championship, but sold his shares in November 2026. He purchased shares in Chelsea later that month.

Lewis Hamilton -- Denver Broncos

The Broncos' ownership group added racing royalty in August 2022. Formula One driver Lewis Hamilton has a stake with the Walton-Penner group, which purchased the team in June 2022.

Hamilton, 37, has the Formula One record for most race wins and has won the Formula One title seven times. The ownership group, which purchased the team for $4.65 billion, is led by Walmart heir Rob Walton and includes former U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice, who also has a stake.

In April, Hamilton joined with Serena Williams in a consortium led by former Liverpool chairman Martin Broughton in an attempt to buy Premier League club Chelsea.

"He is a champion competitor who knows what it takes to lead a winning team," Walton said in a statement.

Marshawn Lynch -- Seattle Kraken

Lynch spent 13 seasons in Seattle with the Seahawks, but his new sports venture in the state of Washington is on the ice. On April 18, he joined the Seattle Kraken ownership team as a minority investor. The former NFL running back will be a part of the NHL's "Hockey is for Everyone" campaign and Kraken owner Tod Leiweke said Lynch expressed interest in shadowing him to learn hockey CEO operations.

"This is something I never would have imagined," Lynch said to CNBC in a statement. "I always dreamed of playing on a professional team but owning one is something special. As I look back on some of my accomplishments...I'm [going to] continue to count my blessings."

Grammy Award-winning artist and Seattle native Macklemore also joined the Kraken ownership team with Lynch.

Wayne Gretzky, Steve Nash and Dustin Johnson -- Las Vegas Desert Dogs

Wayne Gretzky is a big lacrosse guy? Yep, you read that right. The Great One may have made his name on the ice, but before Gretzky was the pride of the Edmonton Oilers he was a bona fide lax bro.

"The national sport of Canada is box lacrosse," Gretzky said. "I started playing lacrosse on a team at the age of six and played all the way until I was 16 years old. I have a great love for the game in the sense I really think that box lacrosse was such a crucial part of the success I ultimately had in ice hockey."

Because of this, it shouldn't be completely surprising that the hockey legend is linking up with 2020 Masters champion Dustin Johnson, NBA Hall of Famer and current Brooklyn Nets head coach Steve Nash and Nets owner Joe Tsai as part of a star-studded ownership group for the National Lacrosse League's newest expansion team in Las Vegas, the Desert Dogs.

Dwyane Wade -- Utah Jazz

Seeing Dwyane Wade support any team other than the Miami Heat is decidedly jarring. In April, the three-time NBA champion purchased an ownership stake in the Utah Jazz, joining majority owner and team governor Ryan Smith, and expressed a desire to take an active role in the franchise. D. Wade made good on his promise. He could be seen courtside throughout the season; he took action when an unsettling fan incident went down during the postseason, and he became a mentor to then-Jazz star Donovan Mitchell.

The former Miami Heat star also added to his portfolio with something a bit closer to home. Wade, a Chicago native, joined the ownership group of the WNBA's Chicago Sky.

"It's a great opportunity to be a part of the league in its very early stages. ... Growth is going to happen, and so I want to be a part of the growth of this league," Wade said.

Kevin Durant -- Philadelphia Union, NJ/NY Gotham FC

In June 2020, Brooklyn Nets star Kevin Durant purchased a 5% stake in MLS' Philadelphia Union, and he has an option to purchase an additional 5% at a later date. Durant also had engaged in talks about purchasing part of D.C. United the year prior, but he said the discussion never progressed.

Durant expanded his portfolio in May of this year, after being named as a minority owner of the National Women's Soccer League (NWSL) club NJ/NY Gotham FC.

Thirty Five Ventures (35V), a company co-founded by the two-time NBA champion and entrepreneur Rich Kleiman, made a significant investment to acquire a stake in the club, marking the company's second investment in a professional soccer team.

Renee Montgomery -- Atlanta Dream

Former Atlanta Dream guard Renee Montgomery made history in February as part of a three-member investor group that was approved to purchase the team. Montgomery is the first former player to become both an owner and executive of a WNBA franchise. The ownership change followed pressure on former Republican Sen. Kelly Loeffler to sell her share of the Dream, after she angered WNBA players with her opposition to the league's racial justice initiatives.

Patrick Mahomes -- Kansas City Royals

Patrick Mahomes is no stranger to winning. While the Kansas City Royals can't exactly say the same, you can't rule out that the quarterback's winning ways might rub off on the franchise now that he is part of their ownership group. If Mahomes' status as an icon in Kansas City was in question (it wasn't), this move surely cemented it. Becoming a baseball owner made sense on several levels for the Chiefs' QB1. Not only was Mahomes -- who played baseball in college -- a legitimate pro prospect, his father, Pat Mahomes, spent 11 seasons in Major League Baseball. He also had to find some way to put that $503 million contract extension to good use.

Venus and Serena Williams -- Miami Dolphins, Angel City FC

Winning major titles and making history, that's what the Williams sisters do. In 2009, Venus and Serena became the first Black female minority owners in the NFL by purchasing a part of the Miami Dolphins. Musicians Jimmy Buffett, Gloria and Emilio Estefan, Fergie and Marc Anthony also bought shares in the team -- the Dolphins' ownership group is nothing if not eclectic. Then, last year, Serena Williams became part of the star-studded Angel City FC ownership group bringing a NWSL team to Los Angeles in 2022.

Mia Hamm, Abby Wambach and Julie Foudy -- Angel City FC

When Angel City FC arrived on the scene it did so in style. Before we even knew the Los Angeles based NWSL club's name, we knew it had superstar backing like no other. Among the 14 former USWNT players who are part of the group are Mia Hamm, Abby Wambach and Julie Foudy. I would have named Lauren Holiday, Shannon Boxx, Rachel Buehler, Amanda Cromwell, Joy Fawcett, Tisha Venturini Hoch, Angela Hucles, Shannon MacMillan, Saskia Webber and sisters Lorrie Fair Allen and Ronnie Fair Sullins, but I was really trying to stay true to my whole "I'm only going to name 20 athletes" thing from the intro. There are also a bunch of celebrities in the mix, but we don't have that kind of time.

Michael Jordan -- Charlotte Hornets

While we're on the subject of owners who haven't had the type of success we grew accustomed to in their playing days, I would be remiss if I didn't mention the GOAT. In 2010, Michael Jordan became the first ex-player to be a majority owner in the league when the NBA's Board of Governors unanimously approved his $275 million bid to buy the then Charlotte Bobcats in his home state of North Carolina. After a decade of underwhelming years, things look to be on the up for the now Hornets with Rookie of the Year LaMelo Ball providing a long-awaited spark in the organization. Never forget when his dad said he could beat MJ one-on-one ... good times.

Alex Rodriguez -- Minnesota Timberwolves, Minnesota Lynx

I don't know what part of this purchase feels less ideal to me, that Alex Rodriguez and his 50-50 business partner Marc Lore are only pursuing acquiring the Minnesota Timberwolves and Lynx after their original plan to buy the New York Mets failed or that Timberwolves star Anthony Edwards had no idea who former MLB star A-Rod was. Either way, the $1.5 billion deal is expected to close around July 1.

David Beckham -- Inter Miami

David Beckham, iconic soccer player and remains-to-be-seen owner. Beckham -- who is incredibly hands on with the franchise -- is part of an ownership group which was initially called Miami Beckham United but now operates under the name Miami Freedom Park LLC. Beckham and Inter Miami have seemingly been riddled with controversy since the club's inception in 2018. But all those problems could be a thing of the past if Lionel Messi decides to head to MLS. Hey, stranger things have happened.

LeBron James -- Liverpool

Back in 2011, LeBron James and manager Maverick Carter became minority owners of Premier League club Liverpool after Fenway Sports Group, which purchased the team in 2010, became the sole marketer of James' global rights. The deal has turned out to be pretty lucrative for James -- his original stake in the club, valued at about $6.5 million, had grown to about $32 million as of 2018. In 2019, Liverpool won the Premier League for their first top-flight league title in thirty years.

James Harden -- Houston Dynamo, Houston Dash

James Harden might not be in Houston anymore, but the former Rockets superstar's presence is still felt in the city. The Beard purchased a 5% stake in the group that controls MLS' Houston Dynamo and NWSL's Houston Dash in 2019. Boxer Oscar De La Hoya is also part of the group. The Dash won their first NWSL title last year, so he's probably feeling pretty good about that investment.

Russell Wilson and Ken Griffey Jr. -- Seattle Sounders

What do Russell Wilson, Ken Griffey Jr. and Macklemore have in common? They are all part of the Seattle Sounders' ownership group. Wilson, along with his wife, musician Ciara, purchased a stake in the team in 2019 -- just in time for them to win an MLS Cup title. Griffey Jr. and his family followed suit in November 2020.

Zlatan Ibrahimovic -- Hammaraby

Seemingly everything Zlatan does makes people react intensely, and that remained true when he purchased part of Swedish team Hammaraby back in 2019. Fans of Malmo, another Swedish team where Zlatan started his professional career, reacted by vandalizing a statue of Zlatan outside the team's home stadium, placing a toilet seat around one of its arms.

Magic Johnson -- Los Angeles Dodgers

Big LA guy. In 2012, Lakers great Magic Johnson was part of a group that bought the Los Angeles Dodgers from Frank McCourt for a record $2 billion. At the time, the price shattered the mark for a sports franchise. Magic kept it real at the time of purchase when explaining his role in recruiting free agents, saying that while he can't talk hitting or pitching with players, he "can talk winning." If recent history is any indication (in case you blacked out all of 2020 -- the Dodgers won the World Series), it worked.

stories.headline: Kangaroos bounce Kiwis for fourth-straight Rugby League World Cup title
stories.summary: The Kangaroos have won a fourth-straight Rugby League World Cup, toppling New Zealand 32-12 in Brisbane.
stories.body:
The Kangaroos have punished a disappointing New Zealand, with Reece Walsh running riot in a 32-12 World Cup final waltz.

There was an expectation the Kiwis, searching for their second Cup title and first since 2008, would push Australia all the way after a two-point loss in a pulsating tournament opener.

But the visitors struggled from the outset in Brisbane on Sunday night, Jamayne Isaako's kick-off floating long in a sign of things to come.

Walsh dazzled at fullback for the Kangaroos, his pace, vision and wicked footwork too much as he helped lay on two tries and generally wreak havoc around the ruck and close to the line.

Conversely, Walsh's New Zealand opposite Kalyn Ponga -- International Rugby League's Golden Boot winner on Thursday night -- was unable to get into game.

Australian hooker Harry Grant and halves Tom Dearden and Cam Munster completely outplayed their error-riddled opposites, while the Kangaroos' pack muscled up.

Dearden laid on two first-half tries for Liam Martin with well-timed short balls, while Bradman Best was rewarded for an inspired chase-down tackle of Jahrome Hughes with a try soon after.

When Tom Trbojevic scored to begin the second half it was 28-6 and effectively game over.

Jack Bostock completed his breakout season with a try in each half for Australia.

It was the Kangaroos' fourth consecutive title and 10th in the last 11 tournaments, dating back to 1975.

stories.headline: Trevor Lawrence, Liam Coen share the blame for the Jaguars' loss to the Giants
stories.summary: The offense struggled mightily in New York. What does Jacksonville need to fix ahead of the Week 12 matchup against the Titans?
stories.body:
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. - Jacksonville Jaguars quarterback Trevor Lawrence shouldered a lot of the blame for his team's poor offensive performance against the New York Giants on Sunday.

It wasn't pretty: two interceptions on two badly thrown passes, two dropped shotgun snaps, three sacks and just one touchdown drive. He looked unsure and confused and didn't play anything like the quarterback who had thrown seven touchdown passes and just one interception while the Jaguars were scoring 115 points in the three previous games.

"I played really, really poorly today, and you're not going to win many games if I don't play better than that," he said after the Jaguars' 23-18 loss to the Giants at MetLife Stadium. "So, I take a lot of it on myself. I did not make enough plays or enough of the routine plays, easy ones. I'm really frustrated with my performance.

"Like I said, it starts with me. I can't play like I did tonight. We're going to be fine moving forward, but we've got to learn from it and get better."

Lawrence threw for 301 yards, but 195 of that came in the second half. He did get the Jaguars into the red zone six times, but they managed only one touchdown. He also made the wrong read on a fourth-and-1 play from the New York 11-yard line and turned the ball over on downs in the third quarter. And he and receiver Jakobi Meyers weren't on the same page on a throw in the third quarter that sailed over Meyers' head and was intercepted, a turnover that led to a Giants field goal.

It's the first time he has thrown multiple interceptions in a game since he threw three against Arizona in Week 12 last season, a game the Jaguars won in overtime.

"It felt like we were on our heels a little bit, and it starts with me," said Lawrence, who completed 25 of 47 passes. "I just thought I didn't get in the rhythm, moreso on my own doing. I just made some mistakes and didn't settle in early. I didn't feel like I saw it good today at all until later in the game.

"I've got to watch the tape to see some of [the mistakes], but some of them I know were just bad plays where I've got to play better and give our team a chance to win."

It was just the Jaguars' third loss in their past 18 regular-season games. They're still 7-3 and atop the AFC South, so the season certainly isn't in jeopardy. But with games against the Chicago Bears, Pittsburgh Steelers and Houston Texans in the next month, Lawrence and the Jaguars' offense cannot afford a repeat of what happened on Sunday.

"We didn't play complementary football," head coach Liam Coen said. "We turned it over, they scored points. We get turnovers, we didn't score points. I felt like you hold a team to 23 points in the National Football League, you should win some of those games."

Two other reasons the offense struggled on Sunday: lack of production in the red zone and not converting on third and fourth downs.

The Jaguars had scored touchdowns on 64.3% of their drives that reached the red zone before Sunday. That ranked 12th in the NFL, but after scoring just one touchdown on six drives against the Giants they dropped to 55.9% (18th).

Jacksonville kicked four field goals, scored one touchdown (Lawrence's 18-yard pass to Brian Thomas Jr.), and turned the ball over on downs. One of those field goals came after an incompletion to Parker Washington in the back of the end zone -- a play that the Jaguars challenged and lost -- and another came on their final possession of the game.

Coen took the blame for the red zone struggles.

"Last week, we kind of struggled early in the red zone because I felt like I called a couple bad runs last week in Tennessee, so we wanted to throw it a little bit more in this game plan in the red zone," he said. "Hindsight looking at it, probably needed to run it a little bit more once we got into the red zone especially. I didn't love some of my calls on the first drive where we busted the short-yardage run and then went pass, pass, pass there. That's not good. That's on me.

"So, I think I didn't help them, and then I think we missed a few things as well, specifically on fourth down where I think we had something there, but at the end of the day when the offense does not perform at the level that it's supposed to, it falls on me."

It didn't help the Jaguars were a combined 6-for-17 on converting third and fourth downs. They were particularly bad on third down (5-for-15), partly because they needed 10 or more yards to convert on seven of those third downs. The Jaguars were 1-for-2 on fourth down, converting one on a 21-yard run by Chris Rodriguez Jr. The other attempt failed on Lawrence's bad read from the New York 11-yard line.

It's also hard to get into any rhythm offensively when eight of the team's 13 penalties came on that side of the ball.

"That's always tough, just hurting ourselves at times," Washington said. "But I know as a team, the main thing, we just need to respond, and we know we can come out next week ready to go."

The good thing for the Jaguars? Next week's opponent is the Tennessee Titans at home at EverBank Stadium, where they're averaging 32.3 points and 372 yards per game this season.

"We're going to be fine moving forward, but we've got to learn from [Sunday] and get better," Lawrence said.

stories.headline: Philadelphia's Cavan Sullivan wins MLS Young Player of the Year award
stories.summary: Philadelphia Union midfielder Cavan Sullivan has been selected as the MLS Young Player of the Year for his breakthrough performance as a 17-year-old.
stories.body:
Philadelphia Union midfielder Cavan Sullivan has been selected as the MLS Young Player of the Year for his breakthrough performance as a 17-year-old.

The award honors the top player who was born Jan. 1, 2004 or later. Sullivan is the youngest player ever to win the award.

Red Bull New York had the runner-up and third-place finishers in the voting. Julian Hall finished second and Adri Mehmeti was third.

Sullivan had nine goals and 14 assists over 28 games in his first MLS season as a full-time player. He had either a goal or an assist in 10 straight matches, the longest such streak by a teenager in MLS history.

Sullivan was called up to the United States men's national team in September and became the second-youngest player in U.S. history to start a match.

MLS players vote on this award along with club technical staff and media.

stories.headline: Too-early NBA All-Star picks: The 24 most deserving players right now
stories.summary: So what if the All-Star Game is three months away? We're picking locks and position battles to watch across both conferences.
stories.body:
There's a lot a basketball to be played before the 2027 NBA All-Star Game tips off in Phoenix on Feb. 21, but it's never too early to start surveying the field. With more than a month of regular-season games on the books, here's a rundown of the 12 most deserving candidates from each conference.

These picks were made to reward games played through Sunday and are not intended to be a projection of the rosters, which won't be announced until the new year. Criteria for selection included health, individual production, impact on winning and team success.

Note: Picks conform to the NBA's 2026 mandate of at least eight international players among the 24 selections. The NBA has not yet announced whether last year's "U.S. vs. the World" tournament format will return.

Jump to a conference:

East | West

Eastern Conference All-Stars
Giannis Antetokounmpo, Heat

The "Greek Freak" is back on track in South Beach after a contentious final season with the Milwaukee Bucks. Antetokounmpo, who ranks in the top five leaguewide in scoring and rebounding, is guiding the No. 6 offense that has ironed out some of its wrinkles after a rough opening week.

While there was some cause for concern that a string of lower-body injuries might limit his effectiveness, the 31-year-old forward remains a forces going downhill to the rim. Antetokounmpo is tied for second in dunks and is shooting 72.2% in the basket area. While the two-time MVP has enjoyed perfect availability to start the season, his health deserves continued scrutiny; he has missed or barely played in three of the last four All-Star Games due to injuries.

Cade Cunningham, Pistons

Cunningham has picked up right where he left off during the Pistons' 60-win campaign in 2025-26, with one noticeable improvement. The 25-year-old guard is back as Detroit's offensive playmaker, ranking in the top 10 in scoring and assists. But after struggling with ball-control issues in last year's playoffs, he is averaging a career-low 3.1 turnovers per game. In one of the most impressive individual efforts of the young season, Cunningham posted 52 points, 11 assists and no turnovers in a Nov. 12 double-overtime win over the Washington Wizards.

Thanks to Cunningham's extraordinary offensive impact and an elite team defense, the Pistons have weathered the early-season absence of center Jalen Duren and the offseason departure of Tobias Harris to remain in the East's playoff picture.

Tyrese Maxey, 76ers

The 26-year-old Maxey is the youngest and least accomplished of Philadelphia's four stars, but he would be the first pick if they were all placed into a fantasy draft. The two-time All-Star is the leading scorer and most reliable night-to-night producer for the 76ers, who sit atop the East standings after adding LeBron James and Jaylen Brown during the offseason.

The not-so-secret key to Philadelphia's early success is its 12-0 record in clutch games. Maxey ranks third leaguewide in plus-minus during clutch situations, and his late-game brilliance was pivotal in wins over the Indiana Pacers and the Cleveland Cavaliers.

Jayson Tatum, Celtics

Tatum hasn't quite fully returned to his pre-Achilles tear form, but he's still been awfully good. The six-time All-Star has reestablished himself as the No. 1 option for a potent Boston offense and joins Luka Doncic as the only players averaging at least 26 points, six rebounds and six assists per game.

Tatum's career-high free throw rate is an especially positive indicator for his recovery and a welcome development for the Celtics' outside-in offense, which lost Brown over the summer. After finishing last in free throw attempts in 2025-26, Boston is up to 26th to start this campaign. The Celtics are back in the East's top tier, but there's room to climb higher if Tatum's outside shooting efficiency returns to his career standard.

Karl-Anthony Towns, Knicks

Towns has channeled his disappointment at not receiving a contract extension last offseason into exceptional all-around play. While some of his teammates have battled malaise at the start of what figures to be a grueling title defense, Towns ranks in the top five at his position by player efficiency rating (PER) and win shares.

The 31-year-old center has helped compensate for Mitchell Robinson's offseason departure with a career-high 13.9 rebounds per game, and he leads the NBA with 16 double-doubles. As the Knicks search for more reliable contributions from Josh Hart and Mikal Bridges, Towns has easily boasted the best net rating among New York's starters.

Jalen Brunson, Knicks

The 2026 Finals MVP accepted responsibility for the Knicks' 0-3 start -- "Everything falls on my shoulders," he said -- and he has been instrumental in stabilizing the team in recent weeks. New York's offensive efficiency has fallen well short of the level of its 2025-26 championship campaign, but Brunson has lifted it back into the top 10 over the past 10 games.

Brunson, 30, continues to rank among the league's top 10 scorers and is second in time of possession. So far, he is holding up well despite that high-usage role and his struggling teammates: The three-time All-Star hasn't missed a game and has upped his scoring and 3-point efficiency from last season.

Donovan Mitchell, Cavaliers

The Cavaliers' stars all share blame for the team's thoroughly mediocre start after their conference finals appearance last season. James Harden was playing sluggish and sloppy basketball until he broke out with a 51-point effort against the Pacers on Friday, and Evan Mobley might never escape his cutting "18 and 8" nickname on social media.

Mitchell remains the leading scorer on a top-five Cleveland offense, though his production has slipped slightly as compared with that of last season. While there is a bigger conversation brewing about how Cleveland might pivot if it takes a step back in the playoffs, Mitchell's 24/4/5 averages look good enough to land his eighth straight All-Star selection.

Jaylen Brown, 76ers

When judging Brown's acclimation to Philadelphia after a blockbuster summer trade, one must differentiate between his strange off-court comments and his solid on-court play. Brown's passive-aggressive statements about Tatum blew up in his face when he played poorly in his first head-to-head matchup against his former teammate.

That sequence of events hasn't been representative of Brown's start in Philadelphia. He has slotted in nicely as a sturdy second option for the 76ers, who have kept winning despite poor shooting from Joel Embiid and inconsistent impact from James. Brown occupied a range of offensive roles during his 10 years in Boston, and that flexibility has been an asset since his big move.

Franz Wagner, Magic

The eight names listed above were all no-brainer picks as established All-Stars on winning teams.

Wagner breaks from that pattern as an aspiring first-time selection whose Magic have been digging out of a 2-7 start. The German forward was on track to be an All-Star two years ago before he was sidelined by an oblique injury, and he has been even better this season in Paolo Banchero's absence (ankle).

The 25-year-old Wagner is posting career highs in scoring, rebounds and assists, and he has demonstrated significant growth as a playmaker under new coach Sean Sweeney. After averaging fewer than four assists per game during his first five seasons, Wagner is one of only five players averaging at least eight assists this season.

Filling the final few slots on the East ballot requires some compromises: The top remaining candidates are mostly secondary options on winning teams or leading options on losing teams.

Paul George, Celtics

George has been one of the league's best second options since landing in Boston as part of the return for Brown. The 36-year-old forward has been a natural fit supporting Tatum in the Celtics' 3-point-heavy offense: George is one of only four qualified players shooting better than 40% on at least eight 3-point attempts per game.

While George wasn't a serious All-Star candidate during his two seasons in Philadelphia, he has reentered the conversation thanks to his positive two-way impact. George's plus-16.7 net rating leads Boston's starters and represents one of the best figures among NBA stars. Who saw that coming?

Scottie Barnes is a more imposing player than George and has better individual numbers, but the Toronto Raptors have struggled on both ends in Kawhi Leonard's absence. Barnes' case has also been held back by a groin injury.

Anthony Davis, Wizards

Davis falls neatly into the "leading option on losing team" category because his strong individual play hasn't been enough to propel the new-look Wizards into the East's playoff picture. Still, he joins Antetokounmpo and Victor Wembanyama as the only players averaging at least 25 points and 9 rebounds per game, and Davis has bounced back from an injury-plagued campaign to rank in the top 10 in PER.

Projecting Davis as an All-Star is a conscious decision not to blame him for Trae Young's terrible start in Washington or the Wizards' roster conflicts. Davis has been significantly more productive than Cleveland's Mobley and Miami's Bam Adebayo, who are among the East's other big man candidates. Davis' strong numbers and good health to date beg the question: Will he still be on the Wizards by the time All-Star Weekend rolls around?

Jalen Johnson, Hawks

Philly's James wouldn't qualify for his 23rd consecutive All-Star Game on this ballot. The 41-year-old forward is averaging career lows in points and PER, and he is enduring his worst shooting season since his rookie year. Maxey and Brown are more deserving candidates for the 76ers, who haven't been dominant enough to warrant three selections.

With that said, no one should be surprised if James ultimately lands a spot. The four-time MVP remains one of the league's most popular players, and he was selected as a reserve via the coaches' vote last season despite missing the first 14 games with sciatica.

But the final spot here went to Johnson, who is off to a slower-than-expected start after earning his first All-Star nod last season. The Hawks are a tricky team to reward because they are so deep and balanced: Johnson is their most productive all-around player, guard Nickeil Alexander-Walker is their leading scorer and defensive stopper Dyson Daniels boasts the best net rating in their starting lineup.

Johnson should emerge as Atlanta's most logical representative assuming his poor shooting numbers improve as the season unfolds. If that doesn't happen, Adebayo, Barnes and Miami's Davion Mitchell are the most enticing alternatives.

Western Conference All-Stars
Victor Wembanyama, Spurs

No explanation needed. But let's run through the absurdity of Wembanyama's start anyway.

He is averaging nearly a point per minute, leads the NBA in dunks and is powering a top-five offense. The French center also sits atop the league in blocks for the fourth straight season as the anchor for a top-five defense. With that level of dominance on both ends, it's no surprise that Wembanyama ranks first in PER, win shares, box plus-minus and just about every other advanced metric.

Through his first 17 games, Wembanyama has been a blowout architect with a jaw-dropping plus-28.5 net rating. The only thing preventing him from posting even more ludicrous numbers is San Antonio's cautious decision to limit him to 30.3 minutes per game.

Luka Doncic, Lakers

To this point, Doncic has been the only person preventing Wembanyama from running away with MVP honors. The Slovenian guard's offensive wizardry has the Lakers rivaling the Spurs at the top of the West standings despite losing James and several other veterans over the summer.

The NBA's scoring leader has already torched rival defenses for seven 40-point performances and two 50-pointers, and Doncic's 37.2 points per game average is the highest mark since the 1960s. Doncic, 27, looks fit and motivated after a hamstring injury cut short his 2025-26 campaign, and he has maintained excellent availability while posting one of the highest usage rates in league history.

Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, Thunder

Gilgeous-Alexander has found this season to be much tougher sledding than his back-to-back MVP campaigns in 2024-25 and 2025-26. After losing three key teammates in offseason trades and three more to major early-season injuries, the ever-steady Canadian guard has done his best to keep Oklahoma City above water as the NBA's second-leading scorer.

What's more, Gilgeous-Alexander is on track to join Wilt Chamberlain and Michael Jordan as the only players to average at least 30 points per game in five straight seasons. But that individual excellence has only translated to an average team offense, and the Thunder will be hard-pressed to make another deep playoff run unless Chet Holmgren (knee) and Cason Wallace (shoulder) are able to recover from their health challenges.

Alperen Sengun, Rockets

Trivia time: Who is the leading scorer for the NBA's most efficient offense?

Somehow, the answer is Sengun, who is posting a career-best 22.1 points per game for a balanced Rockets attack that has all five starters averaging in double digits.

While Fred VanVleet's return from injury has shifted Kevin Durant into a slightly lower-usage role, the 24-year-old Sengun has remained a central part of Houston's offense. The Turkish big man ranks in the top five leaguewide by PER and win shares, and he has dished more assists than any center besides, well ...

Nikola Jokic, Nuggets

Jokic's historic production has shown modest signs of slippage in his age-31 season: He is shooting a career-low 30.2% on 3-pointers, he is scoring less frequently in the basket era, his rebounding rate is down and he has fallen outside the top five in PER and win shares.

While the Serbian center might not finish first or second in MVP voting for the first time since 2019-20, he's still a no-brainer All-Star who squeezes the most possible wins out of an unremarkable supporting cast. Jokic is on pace to lead the league in assists for the second straight season, and Denver's outlook has gradually improved since its lackluster 3-3 start.

Jamal Murray, Nuggets

Like Jokic, Murray has done everything in his power to keep Denver afloat. The Canadian guard has surpassed his longtime teammate to lead the Nuggets in scoring for the first time in his 10-year career, and he is posting career highs in PER and true shooting percentage. Murray's 51/47/88 shooting splits are Stephen Curry-esque.

The sustainability of Denver's approach will draw scrutiny as the season unfolds. Jokic and Murray both rank in the top five leaguewide in minutes per game, and the Nuggets lack credible alternatives to lighten their loads. Even if Denver eventually unravels, there's something gallant about watching Jokic and Murray fight to extend their title-contention window.

Deni Avdija, Trail Blazers

Avdija earned his first All-Star selection last season, but there was reason to be worried that his impact might be blunted by the additions of Damian Lillard and Ja Morant. The Israeli forward has put those concerns to bed with another stellar campaign, striking an excellent partnership with Lillard that has sustained Portland through Morant's early-season hamstring injury.

There's nothing subtle about Avdija's game: He seeks to punish opposing defenses with an onslaught of dribble drives, and he has complemented his typical brass knuckles approach with the best outside shooting season of his career. Other than the Grizzlies, Avdija's Blazers have been the league's biggest overachievers to date.

Ty Jerome, Grizzlies

Barring a rash of injuries, there won't be many spots for first-time selections in the West. Even so, Jerome will be hard to snub if he and Memphis continue this surprising run. The 29-year-old guard hasn't previously been a serious All-Star candidate during a circuitous career that has included multiple stops in the G League, but he has exploded onto the scene as the leading scorer for the NBA's second-ranked offense.

The Grizzlies have emerged as the league's most pleasant surprise thanks to innovative coach Tuomas Iisalo, a strong rookie campaign from Cameron Boozer and vital contributions from the NBA's highest-scoring bench. Jerome stands out within that impressive collective, averaging a career-high 24.8 points per game while ranking in the top 20 leaguewide by PER.

Cooper Flagg, Mavericks

Flagg looks poised to become the fifth No. 1 pick since 2000 to earn All-Star honors in his age-20 season, joining James, Davis, Zion Williamson and Mavericks teammate Kyrie Irving. The Maine native has been on the fast track since high school, and his immediate impact has helped lift the retooling Mavericks into the West's play-in tournament race.

Last season's Rookie of the Year is averaging 24.3 points, 6.3 rebounds and 6.4 assists per game, numbers not posted by such a young player since James and Doncic. Flagg's offensive game is an interesting mix of traditional and modern elements: He is excellent at getting to the free throw line and hitting from the midrange, but his 3-point efficiency and volume at the rim need improvement.

LaMelo Ball, Timberwolves

The Wolves have chugged along as one of the West's best teams even though franchise guard Anthony Edwards played only four games before undergoing knee surgery. Minnesota has two strong candidates to fill Edwards' spot: Ball, a flashy guard who arrived from Charlotte in an offseason trade, and veteran center Rudy Gobert, who has captained the NBA's top-ranked defense.

Both have made indispensable contributions to Minnesota's success. Ball has kept the offense humming and lightened the mood, while Gobert has positioned himself for his 10th All-Defensive selection with steady doses of rim protection and rebounding. Ball, 25, earned the nod here for helping to get the most out of Ayo Dosunmu -- who has stepped into the starting lineup in Edwards' absence -- and forward Jonathan Kuminga, another offseason addition who has exceeded expectations.

Kevin Durant, Rockets

The field for the West's final two All-Star spots has been thinned out by injuries to Edwards, Lakers guard Austin Reaves, Spurs guard Dylan Harper and the Thunder's Jalen Williams and Holmgren. From that group, Reaves is best positioned to make a speedy return and claim a spot.

For now, Durant narrowly edged out Minnesota's Gobert, Portland's Lillard and Phoenix's Devin Booker. The 38-year-old forward has ceded some authority in Houston's offense but has maintained 51/40/88 shooting splits and a healthy plus-8.3 net rating.

The quality of Durant's contributions remains high, even if his 21.0 points per game are the fewest since his rookie campaign. Houston's league-leading offense, which ground down in last year's playoffs, needs Durant's gravity to thrive, and he has led the Rockets in minutes despite being by far the team's oldest player.

Stephen Curry, Warriors

Unlike the other 23 names on this list, Curry is currently sidelined for an extended period due to injury. But the two-time MVP earned a tribute vote on this ballot for his astonishing start to his 18th season.

Before suffering an oblique tear earlier this month, the 38-year-old Curry had turned back the block and was scoring and drilling 3-pointers like he did back in the mid-2010s. What's more, Golden State has been barely functional without its franchise icon: The Warriors are just 4-7 without him, including a 1-4 skid since his injury.

Sadly, Curry's torrid opening month proved too good to be true. If he can't ramp back up to full speed by the time the real All-Star ballots are due, Reaves projects as a worthy replacement. The 28-year-old guard has averaged a career-high 24.7 points per game as Doncic's sidekick in a Lakers offense that has shredded most of its early-season competition.

stories.headline: MLB free agency tracker: 2026-27 offseason trades, moves
stories.summary: We've got you covered on all the major MLB hot stove signings and trades.
stories.body:
The 2026-27 MLB hot stove was lit just days after the Milwaukee Brewers hoisted the franchise's first World Series championship trophy.

All eyes this winter are on the free agency of two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal. But he's not the only one who will make a splash in the market, with Freddy Peralta, Randy Arozarena, Seiya Suzuki and Michael King among the other free agents to watch.

Which teams will go big to contend for the 2027 World Series title? And who will make the trades and signings that have everyone buzzing?

Below is a running list of notable transactions and updates from throughout the MLB offseason.

Grades for every notable offseason move

More: Best fits for top free agents | Latest on Skubal | FA rankings

The New York Mets continued their spending spree Monday by coming to terms on a one-year deal with first baseman Paul Goldschmidt, a source told ESPN.
