stories.headline: Real Madrid's Mourinho: Vinícius Jr. 'doesn't have to be MVP' to deliver
stories.summary: Mourinho has backed Vinícius Júnior to "return to his maximum potential" as Real Madrid face PSV Eindhoven in Champions League play.
stories.body:
José Mourinho has backed Vinícius Júnior to "return to his maximum potential" while stressing that the Real Madrid star "doesn't have to be man of the match" to deliver as they face PSV Eindhoven in the Champions League on Tuesday.

Vinícius has served a four-match domestic ban and lost his place to summer signing Yan Diomande in recent weeks, but impressed off the bench in Madrid's 2-1 win over Celta Vigo on Saturday, playing a part in both goals.

Mourinho has confirmed that the Brazil winger will start against PSV as he continues his quest to find his best form, having opted to stay at Madrid and sign a new long-term deal in the summer.

"I think he'll return to his maximum potential," Mourinho said in a news conference on Monday, when asked if Vinícius, 26, can get back to his best. "He's young. Sometimes when players get close to 30, 32 or 33, they aren't able to maintain the ideal physical level.

"There are players who get to that age and they lose their motivation. But Vini is young... He's won everything. He's a very good boy, very empathetic, and that's fundamental. Now he's had a very positive involvement [against Celta]."

Mourinho pointed to the red-card incident against Villarreal on Oct. 10, when Vinicius scored a crucial goal, only to have it disallowed and then be sent off for a hair-pull in the buildup.

"I remember when he changed the game against Villarreal," the coach said. "He scored what would have been a key goal, and then it was ruled out, and he was four games out. Maybe that interrupted his moment of growth, of confidence returning.

"Tomorrow he plays, and we all expect his best version ... But from my side there's no pressure. There's pressure to work hard -- as he's been doing -- and help the team. For me, if he gives everything, he doesn't have to be the man of the match."

Earlier on Monday, Madrid confirmed that forward Endrick had suffered a muscular injury.

The Brazil international, who has been linked with a move in January to secure more game time, played 19 minutes in Madrid's win over Celta.

"Following tests carried out today on our player Endrick by Real Madrid's medical staff, he has been diagnosed with a muscle injury in the adductor of his left leg," the club said in a brief statement. "His recovery will be monitored."

stories.headline: Winners and losers of the Dylan Larkin trade to the Canadiens
stories.summary: It was a mutually beneficial trade ... with significant aftershocks around the league. Here's what to know.
stories.body:
The Dylan Larkin trade saga finally ended on Sunday night as the Detroit Red Wings traded their former captain to the Montreal Canadiens.

Larkin, a 30-year-old center, was traded along with a 2028 second-rounder and a 2027 third-rounder to the Habs for top center prospect Michael Hage, forward Kirby Dach, goalie Sam Montembeault and first-round picks in 2027 and 2029 that are both top-10 protected, along with a 2027 second-rounder and a fourth-rounder in 2028.

The Canadiens then traded that 2028 second-rounder to the Anaheim Ducks who traded Detroit's 2027 second-rounder, which they acquired in the John Gibson deal, over to Montreal.

Here are the winners and losers of this blockbuster deal in Detroit, Montreal and beyond.

Winner: Montreal's Stanley Cup chances
The Canadiens have a No. 1 center in Nick Suzuki. He posted a 101-point season and won the Selke Trophy as the NHL's best defensive forward last season. His chemistry with Cole Caufield resulted in a 51-goal season for the winger last season.

What they didn't have was much behind him in the depth chart, at least at a championship-contender level. They could have waited for Hage, their top prospect, to incubate into one. But after making the Eastern Conference finals last season, Montreal's Stanley Cup window is open now. Here's the great thing about acquiring Larkin: He's the center for now and four years from now.

His $8.7 million average annual value is locked in through 2030-31. He's part of a parade of sub-$10 million AAVs for Montreal's core of players: Suzuki ($7.875 million), Caufield ($7.85 million) and Lane Hutson ($8.85 million), Noah Dobson ($9.5 million) and Ivan Demidov ($9.15 million). All of them but Suzuki are signed through 2030-31, while his contract is up in 2030. The window isn't just open for Montreal -- it's wide open.

Larkin slides into a second-line role to give Demidov the best center he has ever had, likely with Juraj Slafkovsky on the other wing. That's a heck of a group. With Suzuki, Larkin and Phillip Danault, the Canadiens now have the center depth to compete with Carolina and Florida in the postseason -- and not just this season.

Montreal was the last Canadian team to win the Stanley Cup in 1993. This trade positions them to be the next over the next few seasons.

Loser: Larkin's bank account
Larkin was suspended without pay by the Red Wings on Oct. 29 after informing the Red Wings he would no longer play for the team while awaiting a trade. Larkin had played 10 games for Detroit before he left the team.

When goalie Connor Hellebuyck was suspended by the Winnipeg Jets after failing to report to training camp, a website called Hellebucks.com was created to chronicle how much money he had given up. The total: $927,835.05, before his trade to the Devils.

From the makers of Hellebucks came LarkinLosses.com, which tracked Larkin's salary bunking. The total: an estimated $1,025,343 through 25 days. Guess you can put a price on happiness.

Winner: The Cone of Silence
The Larkin trade to Montreal didn't happen overnight. He had opted to expand his list to include the Canadiens several weeks ago, according to NHL sources. That fact was kept quiet by all involved to allow the process to play out.

It's unclear how long that predated the Red Wings' visit to Montreal on Oct. 10, when Bell Centre fans chanted "We want Larkin!" in an attempt at recruitment. Although one imagines that didn't hurt.

When Larkin first requested a trade from the Red Wings, he was willing to waive his no-trade clause for only three teams: Minnesota, Florida and Vegas. As the process started piling up causalities -- GM Steve Yzerman, Larkin's captaincy and eventually his salary when he was suspended without pay -- Larkin expanded this trade list to include Carolina, Colorado, Dallas, New Jersey, Tampa Bay, Utah and Washington.

And, apparently, Montreal.

It can't be stressed enough how remarkable this process was in its clandestine nature. Montreal was considered, at best, a trade option that Detroit interim GM Shawn Horcoff could only humor if Larkin's will had been broken while suspended. At worst, Montreal was a Canadian city trying to lure a U.S. Olympian to reverse the polarity on that player migration trend. All the while, the two sides were inching toward a trade.

Kudos to the front offices and Larkin's agent, Pat Brisson, for keeping this deal in the hush hush.

Loser: The trade protection 'crisis'
Larkin was one of a handful of players who asked for a trade and then used their contractually negotiated no-trade clauses in an attempt to "force" their way to a desired new location.

Thanks to Larkin, Brady Tkachuk and Connor Hellebuyck, the trend caught the eye of NHL commissioner Gary Bettman.

"This notion now, where you can select where you want to go to and you can demand a trade, that was never the original intention," Bettman said. "If this becomes a problem -- I don't think one offseason a problem makes -- but if it becomes a problem, it's something we are going to have to discuss with the players' association."

Detroit hung tough through Larkin's initial request, and didn't end up trading him to any of the three teams in his short list -- including Minnesota, his top choice. They let it linger through the summer and through training camp and then had him actually return to the lineup before he bailed after 10 games and was suspended without pay.

Even if Montreal was eventually an approved destination, playing in a Canadian city wasn't part of Larkin's ask for months. Does this saga still help build the case against no-trade-clause abuse, or did it end with the Red Wings having some modicum of leverage?

Winner: Acquiring Hage
Hage, 20, returned to the University of Michigan for his junior season to hone some of his defensive skills and has made progress there. Meanwhile, he's still tearing it up offensively with 26 points in 13 games. Drafted 21st overall in 2024 by the Canadiens, he was their center of the future, until he was traded for the center of the present their lineup needed to push for the Cup. And now he's a Wolverine whose rights are held by the Red Wings.

As I reported in the Wysh List last week, reports that the Red Wings were seeking an established 30-goal scorer in exchange for Larkin weren't entirely accurate. One team that checked in on Larkin had Detroit asking for a young cornerstone center who could score 30 goals in the NHL but hadn't yet. Hage is the type of young center for which the Wings were being denied by other teams in the Larkin derby. To get a player like this from Montreal is the centerpiece of the deal.

There are differing opinions on Hage's ceiling in the NHL. Some have him as a future star, others see him as a solid prospect rather than can't-miss. One thing is clear: He'll have more upward mobility on the Detroit depth chart than playing behind Suzuki in Montreal.

Contextually, he's what the Red Wings have been unable to find in the draft lottery or develop internally: a young potential No. 1 center who gives them hope for a better tomorrow, rather than one asking out because of yesterday.

Loser: Acquiring everything else
The rest of this trade is expendable parts and window dressing for Detroit.

Dach, 25, was acquired to fill the No. 2 center role that Montreal just traded him to truly fill. He's injury-prone, having failed to play more than 58 games in any of his four previous seasons with the Canadiens. He's an unrestricted free agent next summer, making him a risky investment or a potential deadline flip for Detroit. Montembeault, 30, is a trade candidate as a fellow UFA.

Montreal wanted to dump both of these contracts, whose cap hits add up to $6.75 million. Did Detroit get enough back for facilitating that?

In quantity, yes. In quality beyond Hage, that's debatable. The Canadiens' pick swap with Anaheim gave them Detroit's second-rounder in 2027. How many spots will that selection be behind Montreal's low first-rounder? Maybe seven at the most? The same math applies to the 2027 second- and third-rounder flips.

The first-rounders, which are the flashiest parts of the trade outside of Hage, are going to be late in the round whether the Red Wings keep them or trade them for more help.

Again, the quantity is impressive for Detroit, given Larkin's trade request and trade protection. But it may not be as needle-moving as it seems beyond Hage.

Winner: Shawn Horcoff
Quantity over quality could still end up being a good thing for Horcoff. The interim GM of the Red Wings found a way to get an impressive return for a captain who quit on his team and had trade protection. When he took over in mid-September, there was finally some thawing between Larkin's camp and Detroit management with regard to broadening his trade horizons.

After that, it was just a matter of landing the plane with the right team, and maximizing the return as best he could. In the process, Horcoff refocused Detroit's trade demands to include less proven NHL prospects, even if that doesn't offer immediate help for this season.

The Larkin trade is an important first step for Horcoff in his attempt to secure the Red Wings' GM job. It gives him some assets with which to work. The next step is finding finality with RFA defenseman Simon Edvinsson, who is also seeking a trade. A suitable return there, and Horcoff has himself a case for permanency. Heck, the fact he was allowed to complete this trade shows a level of trust in him from ownership.

Loser: The Minnesota Wild
The Wild were reportedly Larkin's preferred destination, and why not?

They have the second-highest points percentage in the league standings this season. They have Quinn Hughes, arguably the NHL's best defenseman and a lifelong friend to Larkin. Hughes won a gold medal with Larkin on the men's U.S. Olympic team in February. So did Wild players Brock Faber and Matt Boldy, as well as coach John Hynes (an assistant on that team) and Bill Guerin, Minnesota's president of hockey operations who was the general manager of Team USA.

Despite its success, Guerin's team has been thin in the middle for several seasons. Adding Larkin would have been paramount toward matching the center depth of Vegas, Colorado, Dallas, Edmonton and other contenders. Instead, the search continues.

The Wild were rumored to have offered center Danila Yurov and three first-rounders for Larkin. Whether it was Detroit opting for a better offer or refusing to grant Larkin's trade wish, he's now north of the border rather in the State of Hockey.

Losing Larkin hurts from a lineup perspective. But they also lost a player who, theoretically, could have helped in pending free agent Quinn Hughes' ongoing mental tumult over whether to extend with the Wild -- provided he hasn't already made up his mind, that is.

stories.headline: Man United's heavy Liverpool loss didn't tell us anything new; epic Barça comeback
stories.summary: Pochettino's debut as Man United manager didn't tell us anything we didn't already know when it came to the scale of rebuild required.
stories.body:
The final international break of 2026 is behind us, and the European soccer weekend gave us plenty to discuss about. After stepping down as U.S. men's national team manager to join Manchester United, Mauricio Pochettino saw the scale of his rebuild laid bare after Sunday's 4-0 thrashing at Liverpool in the Premier League's game of the weekend.

In LaLiga, Barcelona made another epic, high-scoring comeback against Villarreal ... and that's almost by design when it comes to how their coach, Hansi Flick, likes his teams to play. We also got big talking points from Bayern Munich (who lost Harry Kane to a long-term injury), Paris Saint-Germain (who also suffered some big injuries), Manchester City (whose identity crisis continues amid the Premier League charges), Inter Milan (who had a major meltdown vs. Atalanta), and much, much more.

It's Monday morning, so what better time for some musings? Let's get into it.

- Pochettino gets reality check as Liverpool ruin his Man United debut

- Olley: Arsenal's near-collapse at Newcastle is a wake-up call

- Dawson: City, Maresca at a crossroads after latest Premier League stumble

What did we learn from Liverpool's 4-0 drubbing of Man United? Very little that we didn't already know...

Yes, there were some curveballs in there, but no real surprises.

I didn't expect new United boss Mauricio Pochettino to set up defensively the way he did, effectively rejiggering Michael Carrick's back line. That was new and a bit weird and totally against conventional wisdom, whereby you don't really want to move pieces around when you're taking over a new club -- especially when you've only had two training sessions and a walk-through. Instead he moved Diogo Dalot back to right back, switched Leny Yoro from right back to centre back and moved Lisandro Martínez from center back to left back. Oh, and he chose to start Matthijs De Ligt, which is its own thing.

Since picking up a serious injury almost a year ago, De Ligt had featured just twice: a disastrous start against Como on Oct. 21 and three minutes of garbage time against Roma before the break. Otherwise, Michael Carrick had kept him under wraps. That Pochettino would pick him to start (at the expense of Harry Maguire) was a curious statement, and it immediately raises the issue of the relationship between the new coach and United's sports science and performance people.

Did the new coach just make up his own mind against their advice? Was it Carrick who wouldn't give De Ligt minutes even though they passed him fit? Whatever the case, the lack of match fitness and chemistry were obvious on the pitch and, in fact, they changed the game.

Whether it was miscommunication with Yoro or misreading the flight of the ball after just eight minutes, the upshot is that the Frenchman was sent off -- harsh? Probably, but decisions on the pitch are king -- and on the ensuing free kick, Dominik Szoboszlai busted through Senne Lammens' horrendous wall to give Liverpool the lead. The game sort of lost a lot of meaning at that point, and things only got worse a few minutes later when Florian Wirtz made it 2-0.

Some United sides of yesteryear might have had a shot at a comeback down a man and two goals with 77 minutes to go at Anfield: this one didn't have a prayer, and nothing we learned from that point onward was going to be new or interesting. Not the lumbering struggles of the Kobbie Mainoo-Youri Tielemans partnership, not the fact that the switch to a back three was going to be like putting a Band-Aid on a leg severed by a shark, not the fact that once Bryan Mbeumo and Matheus Cunha were off the pitch, Bruno Fernandes would be doing his Don Quixote-against-windmills impersonation with only Joshua Zirkzee to play off.

From a United perspective, it is what it is. Anfield away was a budgeted defeat; everything changed after 10 minutes anyway and Pochettino wasn't going to fix things in 72 hours. Move on.

Equally, it's a little tricky to judge Liverpool too. Wirtz and Rio Ngumoha looked good -- really good -- but they won't get to play ten man United every week. The Szoboszlai-Alexis Mac Allister tandem behind four attackers yielded dividends against this bunch, but the jury's out (and, you suspect Ryan Gravenberch, when fit, will be in) against better opponents.

Manager Andoni Iraola sure as heck isn't getting carried away and neither should you. This is a transition season, when his vision of Liverpool comes to fruition, as many as four or five of these players won't be there and the football will be different too. But he's balancing building the approach he wants with grinding out results (they're a point out of second place, for what it's worth) and that's all you can ask of him right now.

Hairy comeback against Villarreal, but this is Flick's Barcelona, for better or worse

At first glance, it seems like a legitimate question. Barcelona go two goals down at home inside of seven minutes and need a late own goal to win, they've conceded 12 times in their last seven games and have kept just one clean sheet in their last eight -- are cracks beginning to appear?

I'm not sure it is that much of an issue. That run of matches includes the Clasico, Paris Saint-Germain away and Atlético Madrid away -- I think we can grade on a curve here. It's worth noting too that against Villarreal, Pau Cubarsí and Anthony Gordon started on the bench, while Rodri and Xavi Espart were unavailable and Lamine Yamal missed a first-half penalty. Tajon Buchanan and Tani Oluwaseyi's goals were improbable strikes made possible by Barca errors and Eric García pointed out at fulltime, the final xG was 3.22 to 0.21 for Flick's crew.

While it's true they showed some rust in the early going, boring as it sounds, I think it's really just an issue of statistical variance. When you play the way Flick does with the personnel he chooses, you take the good with the bad, which means that occasionally you make things easier for the opposition. With a more conservative approach, Fermín López doesn't attempt to pass the ball across the back line. With a veteran centerback who marshals the line better than a recycled midfielder like Frenkie de Jong (and a more reactive fullback than Eric Garcia), maybe you don't get caught out for the second goal.

I made the point before that if Barcelona had allocated their scant transfer resources a little differently -- maybe picking up a standout central defender and/or center forward instead of more hybrid attacking players, and seeing Rodri as the missing link -- perhaps they could play the way they do and do so with more individual quality. But heck, Flick's approach has yielded wins in all but two games this season. Nobody can argue with that.

Man City booed off the pitch after more dropped points and a defensive horrow show vs. Fulham

The numbers keep mounting for Man City. It's now one win in their last six games across all competitions. The last clean sheet was nine games ago and on Saturday, it felt like every turnover in the final third resulted in a clear run at Gianluigi Donnarumma's goal, slicing through midfield and defense.

Credit Fulham, sure -- dare I say it, Alvaro Arbeloa's side have lost just one league game since Sept. 5, which was also the last time they conceded more than a single goal -- but once again, we're seeing the City back line add up to considerably less than the sum of its parts. These are quality defenders who simply haven't found the right chemistry, and it could have been worse without a couple of big Donnarumma saves.

That has to be Enzo Maresca's biggest priority right now, but it's not just about the back four. The midfield was overrun once again and while it's easy to point fingers at Ayyoub Bouaddi, it's worth remembering that he's 19 years old and is new to the country and the Premier League. Maybe we should remind ourselves too how difficult it is to come to England as a teenager and play significant minutes in that position, which he'll have to do as part of a three-man rotation with Elliot Anderson and Enzo Fernández. Indeed, the last teenager to make 30 or more appearances in central midfield after a move from abroad was Roy Keane at Nottingham Forest in the 1980s, and he moved from Cobh Ramblers in Ireland; not quite the same thing. (Cesc Fabregas did it too and was even younger, but he had the benefit of a whole season in Arsenal's academy first.)

Just as disappointing -- and why they were booed at the end presumably -- was the attacking output in the second half. A single shot on target (Anderson's wonder strike) and an xG of 0.31 is not what you expect from City at home.

Arsenal's draw means the deficit is still just six points, which is manageable with so many games to go. But if City are to compete, Maresca needs to find the right formula.

Inter Milan play with fire and get burned in wild 4-4 draw at Atalanta

And no: in case you don't follow Serie A, Gian Luigi Gasperini is long gone, and this isn't the Atalanta of years past. There's a reason they're in the bottom half of the table.

Inter deciding to settle for a point when 3-1 up with 20 minutes to go (and 4-3 up in injury time) hurts, as does the fact that with Lazio (look out for my column on them later this week) and Roma both winning, they slip into third place.

The obvious thing to do here is to blame the defending and to be fair, from Djed Spence to Alessandro Bastoni to Benjamin Pavard, there was no shortage of individual errors at the back, often more mental than technical. They've already conceded 17 goals in 12 league games this season and those aren't title-winning numbers. But it also speaks to the vibe; the drop in intensity was palpable at 3-1 up, almost as if Inter were looking ahead to the midweek Champions League clash. Do that and you get punished.

There are positives, of course. Francesco Pio Esposito bagged a hat trick -- he's up to eight for club and country in his last five games -- and the wonderful thing about the big man is that even when he's not scoring, he contributes in so many different ways. Nicolo Barella was dominant while was on the pitch, and Lautaro Martínez is available again, playing the last 15 minutes after six months out injured.

Now comes the tricky part for Cristian Chivu. He's had success preaching confident, carefree attacking football in line with how the top European sides play. But while Serie A is changing, this is still Italy: defensive blunders and squandered leads still take on outsized importance. He has to stay the course in terms of philosophy, while tightening up the defending. It's not an easy to needle to thread.

Quick hits

10. AS Roma's Malen monsters Parma with some next-level finishing: It's Roma and it's Gasperini in charge, so you expect goals. If you want to nitpick, you can point out that it was 1-1 away to Parma with 20-odd minutes to go and they got lucky that Gianluca Mancini's evident hair-pull on Nesta Elphege wasn't punished with a red card. But really, who wants to talk about that when Roma are a joy to watch and won 5-1, with Donyell Malen scoring four times?

Malen has now scored 34 goals in 41 appearances for Roma since joining from Aston Villa just over 10 months ago for a fee of around €25 million. I think it's pretty evident that we can file it away as a rare Unai Emery transfer blunder. Would he be as productive in a different system, without Gasperini's front-foot-forward style and the likes of Paulo Dybala, Mathias Soule and Rodrigo Mora teeing him up? Who knows? It doesn't really matter though. He's devastating and at times so are Roma, who are now just two points behind city rival (and table-topping) Lazio. They're already counting down the days to the derby on Dec. 18 ...

9. Teen sensation Luca Williams-Barnett lifts Tottenham Hotspur on his full debut, but now let's leave him be: He's been hyped in London youth football circles for the past five years (if not longer) and on Saturday -- his full league debut -- he scored one and set up another as Spurs beat Ipswich Town 2-0. It's inevitable that the hype machine will go into gear, not least because he's been at the club since he was 10 and Spurs legend Kane also scored in his first league start -- he turned out to be pretty good. Williams-Barnett's size, fluidity and technical ability are evident, and he showed no fear against Ipswich, at times taking an undermanned Tottenham on his back.

But let's pump the brakes now. Roberto De Zerbi referenced other teenage prodigies -- like Lamine Yamal and Eden Hazard -- post-game, and he probably wishes he hadn't done so. There are more much-hyped teenage debutants who don't instantly make the grade than those who do. Williams-Barnett deserves time to grow and develop at his own pace.

8. Neither pretty nor popular, but Borussia Dortmund extend their lead at the top of the Bundesliga: Performance-wise, the 1-0 win over Borussia Mönchengladbach wasn't much to write about. Dortmund boss Nico Kovac is still catching strays even as his team moved two points clear of Bayern in first place. (There probably is no top-of-the-table coach who gets more flak than Kovac, who -- gentle reminder -- coaches a team that have won 12 of 16 games in all competitions, losing just once.)

But squint and you see the positives. Fábio Silva was busy in Serhou Guirassy's place. Konstantinos Karetsas is a baller. The much-maligned back three kept a clean sheet. And Felix Nmecha, again, was there to deliver the late three-pointer. Dortmund need to improve if they're to come close to reaching their ceiling; the problem is that sometimes, when you work on your weaknesses in an effort to improve, you end up sacrificing results. Kovac isn't going to do that right now, and you can understand why.

7. Real Madrid make it nine wins in a row, but this was a game to forget: Or, better yet, it was a game from which to learn. Apart from the fullbacks and Aurélien Tchouaméni (replaced by Eduardo Camavinga) this was pretty much the new-found, "balanced" version of Real Madrid at home to Celta Vigo, with Yan Diomande out left and Arda Güler coming in from the right. It made it all the more surprising that they looked wholly unprepared and out of sorts during a first half in which Kylian Mbappé missed a penalty and Celta took the lead (with a gorgeous team goal), very nearly scoring a second.

Jose Mourinho gave them 15 minutes to dig themselves out of their hole and turn the whistles into cheers. When that didn't work (and in fact, Thibaut Courtois had to rescue them again) he brought in the starting full backs and, crucially, Vinícius Júnior. The time away from LaLiga -- he missed four games through suspension -- obviously did Vinícius good as he played a key role in both Jude Bellingham's equalizer and Carlos Espí's late winner. Madrid finished the game with Vinícius and Endrick out wide, Mbappe and Espí through the middle, and Bellingham and Güler in midfield. It's the sort of thing you normally only see in desperation cup second legs, but it speaks to how Mourinho got the "vibe" right. Now he needs to figure out what went wrong in that first half.

6. Brighton's best-laid plans put to waste ... that's football: I really can't fault Fabian Hurzeler for the fact that Brighton lost away to Hull. As the clock hit ninety, the expected goals were 2.23 to to 0.66. They had dominated the game and if Konstantinos Tzolakis -- by the way, between him, Christos Mandas (Lazio) and Odysseas Vlachodimos (Newcastle United), Greek keepers are lighting it up right now -- hadn't been dispensing miracles, they would have been several goals to the good.

Then came the Hull counters (Costinha's sending off didn't help) and those two late, late Oli McBurnie goals. Hurzeler said afterward that they paid a price for continuing to attack in injury time while a man down, which opened them up to counterattacks. What he didn't say -- and what I don't think you'll ever hear him say -- is that it was a mistake to go for it instead of settling for a point. Working for Brighton, he understands the concept of variance and what the analytics say.

5. First Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, now Désiré Doué ... Paris Saint-Germain dealt another ACL blow: You feel for Doué above all, because this could have been his breakout campaign. But football-wise, suffering a season-ending injury in a fairly routine 3-2 win at Nice (not as close as the score suggests, the home side pulled one back in garbage time) now becomes a real issue for Les Parisiens boss Luis Enrique.

Sure, there's plenty of depth in his front three, but now two big pieces are sidelined. And going the rest of the campaign with four guys -- Ousmane Dembélé, Ferran Torres, Maghnes Akliouche and Mika Godts -- to rotate through your forward line is a big ask, especially when three of the four only arrived in the summer. He can try to pull a youngster out of the hat, but more likely he'll ask for a reinforcement in the winter transfer window. Given how impressive PSG have been in the UEFA Champions League, Luis Enrique is not going to pass up the chance of a three-peat.

4. Yes, this season is different, and Arsenal need to put games away: Mikel Arteta's side are substantially better and more settled than everyone else in the Premier League right now. And yet they needed Noni Madueke's strike 12 minutes from time to rescue a point away to Newcastle United, a side that won just one game at home all season. Without Madueke's equalizer, they would have been just four points clear of second place, ahead of a City side firing blanks and, well, Brighton.

That should set off alarm bells, as should the fact that before Madueke's goal, they hadn't managed a single shot of any kind in the second half, while allowing Newcastle -- who admittedly picked up their tempo after the break -- to come back and lead 2-1. They have the same points total as a year ago, but this all feels very different, and not necessarily in a good way. In this context, while Kepa Arrizabalaga is a solid option, they needed David Raya's injury like they needed a hole in the head.

3. Bayern Munich's weekend from hell: It started with the lackluster 1-1 draw at home against FC Cologne, marked by Harry Kane's injury (and confirmation that we're unlikely to see him again until late February). And then Bayern board member Karl Heinz Rummenigge upped the ante on the Jamal Musiala controversy suggesting that his health issues meant his enormous contract might "no longer be justifiable." Musiala has an ongoing neurological issue that caused him to collapse twice on the pitch over the summer.

Cue understandable pushback from manager Vincent Kompany and sporting director Max Eberl, as well as FIFPro, the players' union. You can see the point that Rummenigge (and Uli Hoeness, who started this whole thing) are trying to make: they need to look out for Bayern's interests, and devoting huge resources on someone who may not be able to physically perform requires discussion. Equally, dragging it out in public is not a classy thing to do and might even violate labor laws. As for Kane, you feel for him and his absence is a blow, given the injuries dogging Ismael Saibari and Serge Gnabry as well. The reality is that they had no cover for him to begin with -- neither of the aforementioned too are genuine center forwards -- and it's hard to see how Bayern can avoid signing someone in January, possibly a veteran on loan.

2. Lionel Messi avoiding a red card only fuels notion that MLS is a business: Which, to be fair, they don't shirk from: no relegation, franchises who buy into the league, endless chatter about "valuations," and so on. But what you don't want is a situation where your star player is perceived to get special treatment because he's "good for business," and that's what happens when Messi throws the ball into the face of Gonzalo Tapia -- never mind that the Columbus Crew forward acted a fool -- and doesn't get sent off. It's hard to disagree with Crew head coach Laurent Courtois, speaking after his team's 3-0 away playoff win in Miami, who said: "Everyone knows."

On the other hand, it's hard to understand what his opposite number, Inter Miami CF coach Kily Gonzalez, meant when he said: "I have to think about the situation, the card doesn't change much." Actually, it does, because if Messi is sent off, then he gets suspended and misses the return leg in Columbus. And if Miami suffer defeat there too -- which becomes more likely if Messi isn't there -- then they're out of the playoffs and MLS lose their casual fan meal ticket.

1. Chelsea crash and burn at home, but it can't just be João Pedro's absence: Nor can it just be the state of that back line, an ode to futility. Or a midfield that, once Moisés Caicedo limps off (like he did on Saturday in the 4-1 home defeat to Leeds United) transforms into a turnstile. Xabi Alonso's ship is taking on water on just about every deck, and it's hard to know what to fix first.

I've made the point before that this is a poorly constructed squad, but it's also one that doesn't really work tactically. Having abandoned his back three, his 4-2-3-1 formation still isn't firing, though at least it gets more of his more talented players on the pitch. And maybe, with Emmanuel Emegha (who showed glimpses, scored a great goal and at least is a genuine center forward) up front, things will get easier for the creative types behind him. But there is no excuse for not looking balanced tactically and not having the right chemistry when you don't play European football and have all week to train. For all the mitigating factors, you expect more from Alonso.

stories.headline: Lewis Hamilton: I could have beaten Kimi Antonelli if I was Ferrari No. 1
stories.summary: Lewis Hamilton has said he believes he could have won a record eighth world championship this season if Ferrari had prioritised him over teammate Charles Leclerc.
stories.body:
Lewis Hamilton has said he believes he could have won a record eighth world championship this season if Ferrari had prioritised him over teammate Charles Leclerc.

Hamilton's claim arrived after he tangled with Leclerc for the second time in three races at the Las Vegas Grand Prix -- a flashpoint Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur described as "completely unacceptable." Leclerc was sanctioned by the stewards for his role in the collision.

Hamilton's maiden win for Ferrari at the seventh round of 23 in Barcelona took him 41 points behind Antonelli, and 40 ahead of Leclerc.

And although Hamilton rejected the notion that he ever called on Ferrari to make him its number one driver, the 41-year-old suggested that, with the right backing from his team, he could have afforded Antonelli a proper run for his money.

"I've never asked to be the number one," Hamilton said. "I genuinely haven't. But there was a point in the season where I was 40 points ahead [of Leclerc] and at that point, the fight was with me and Kimi.

"I was the closest one to him. I was second for a long time in the year, and at that point I needed the backing to make sure we beat Kimi.

"There were a few instances in the season -- where, with the support -- I think we could have beaten Kimi in that battle.

"It's not what I've asked for. But we shouldn't have been able to come together [in Las Vegas]. It should just never happen. I've said everything I can on it. And the question now should be for Ferrari."

Hamilton's chances of finishing runner-up in the standings -- his highest championship position since missing out on his eighth title to Max Verstappen in 2021 -- now look shot following the Dutch driver's brilliant recent form.

- Lewis Hamilton, Charles Leclerc 'unmanageable' - Ferrari boss

- Max Verstappen, George Russell's latest war of words unlikely to stay in Vegas

- Max Verstappen mocks George Russell in brutal outburst: 'So far below my level'

Hamilton is 37 points behind Verstappen with only 50 points left across the remaining rounds, in Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

Hamilton is three points clear of both George Russell and Lando Norris, with Leclerc 17 points adrift.

Russell finished only ninth in Sin City after he pranged the barriers with just two laps remaining when a late move on teammate Antonelli for second backfired.

"I wanted that win," Russell said. "It was a bizarre race, and I went for a high-risk move and paid the price.

"Of course I'm disappointed with the outcome, however, I have no regrets. I fought and knew if I wanted the win, I needed to be in the top two positions into the final laps."

stories.headline: Way-too-early look ahead to the 2027 AFL Draft: 15 players to know
stories.summary: The 2027 AFL Draft will look markedly different to the past few years with the introduction of Tasmania. Who are the players to know? Jasper Chellappah has named 15 to keep an eye on next year.
stories.body:
On to the next.

The 2027 AFL Draft will look markedly different to the past few years, with Tasmania's inclusion making for an expansion draft similar to that of 2010 and 2011. The Devils own picks 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, and 13 in the first round, plus the first pick of each subsequent round as part of concessions.

The club will need to trade 5, 7, 11, and 13 or roll them into 2028 or 2029. That means the competition's 19th team will take 1, 3 and 9 to the draft next year.

Tasmania has also pre-listed some of the brightest talents in the crop. Axel Walsh, Baxter Sruk, and Jake Miller were all clear pick No. 1 contenders 12 months out from their draft, and will attend school in Hobart and play football in the VFL next year.

Five Tasmania-tied teens have been included in the ones to watch next year. Another three are club-tied, making 2027 the most compromised draft in AFL history. Twenty-three of the 46 prospects in the AFL Futures exhibition on Grand Final day were club-tied.

Perhaps the saving grace for 18 other clubs is the fact that 2027 has been touted as an elite draft class for some time. There's premium talent still in the open pool and another 12 months for more quality to emerge, with a heavy leaning towards midfielders.

With an extended 15 prospects given the club-tied nature of the class, this is ESPN's way-too-early look ahead to the best prospects in the 2027 AFL Draft.

1. Axel Walsh (Tasmania pre-list)

East Perth/Western Australia

RUC, 201cm

Another in the resurgence of premium ruck prospects in the draft, and perhaps the best. Walsh is a monster in the air; his best traits come with his aerial strength where he drifts back to intercept mark, pushes forward to stretch defences and dominates around the ground. He will fill out to become a true ruck size and is as close to Max Gawn as a prospect has been this decade. Walsh would be the pick one favourite if he wasn't pre-listed by Tasmania.

2. Baxter Sruk (Tasmania pre-list)

Eastern Ranges/Vic Metro

MID, 185cm

Sruk has been a big game performer and consistent midfield standout in the Talent League. He's a physical on-baller that throws his weight around, impacts with his ball-winning and gets forward to kick goals in bunches. Sruk thrives in the heat of the contest and brings tenacity to Tasmania's list.

3. Jake Miller (Tasmania pre-list)

Western Jets/Vic Metro

FWD, 197cm

Miller is the leading key forward prospect next year. He enjoyed a stellar national championships as a bottom-ager, named to the All-Australian team as well as the Talent League All-Australian side. Miller is a brilliant mark with arms outstretched, able to take big contested marks in packs and secure the ball on long searching leads. He's a reliable set shot off his left foot and is an elite runner for his size. Tasmania has already pre-listed the immense talent.

4. Max Thompson

Bendigo Pioneers/Vic Country

FWD/MID, 175cm

Thompson has played in varying positions and looked good but is clearly at his best inside 50. He's smart and crafty, puts speed on the game and is a wonderfully fluid kick of the ball. Thompson can get up the ground and beat his man back to goals, distribute off halfback or win his own ball. He's the type of versatile small forward that clubs will covet.

5. James Artemis

East Fremantle/Western Australia

MID, 177cm

A leading contender in the open pool, Artemis is the cousin of Essendon's Jaxon and will have suitors very early in the draft. He's a hard-nosed contested midfielder that can then link up transition with hard running and slick ball use. He's dogged with the ball up for grabs and then powers through contact to get it moving forward.

6. Koby Bewick (Essendon father-son)

Calder Cannons/Vic Metro

MID, 178cm

Modern footy suits Bewick down to the ground. The son of 1993 and 2000 premiership small forward Darren, the Calder midfielder has been thrown around in different positions but has all the traits to become an excellent on-baller. He's incisive with his movement and foot skills on the outside, and possesses the running base and work ethic to rack up a lot of the ball in transition. He comes alive in open space where he can run and carry and pick out targets inside 50, which could see him start his career off halfback or a wing. Bewick kicked two goals from 19 touches in his Futures outing.

7. Zemes Pilot (Port Adelaide NGA)

South Adelaide/South Australia

FWD/MID, 193cm

Pilot is an elite basketball talent as well, so it's a coup for footy that the 193cm forward is opting to pursue opportunities in Port's NGA. The uber-athletic tall forward is incredible to watch, soaring above packs to take epic marks, breaking ankles with sharp agility and kicking goals from ridiculous angles. He had a game last year in the SANFL U16s with 27 disposals and 9.4 in front of goals.

8. Jett Flower

Eastern Ranges/Vic Metro

MID/DEF, 183cm

Flower is the grandson of Melbourne legend Robbie, and one of the top open pool prospects in 2027. Boasting one of the best names to come through the pathways in some time, Flower is a classy outside midfielder with beautiful foot skills and a strong running base. He likely appeals to clubs as a rebounder out of defence with his competitiveness a feature behind the ball. Flower was best afield in the Futures game with 17 disposals and a goal.

9. Louis Salopek (Port Adelaide father-son)

Dandenong Stingrays/Vic Country

MID/FWD, 186cm

A genuine star of the crop, Salopek has been in the wars across the past year or so, enduring three separate incidents of a collapsed lung. He burst onto the scene for Vic Country in the U16s champs and plays with a high motor, tackling and pressuring through the midfield and pushing forward to hit the scoreboard. He's keen to get to the Power as the son of Steven.

10. Riley Stratford (Tasmania pre-list)

Sandringham Dragons/Vic Metro

MID, 188cm

A taller midfielder who still needs to build into his frame, Stratford has been part of some massive games in his junior career. He was a star for Brighton Grammar on the way to an inaugural APS title and can play on a wing or through the engine room with impact in the air. Tasmania has locked him away and he'll play for their VFL side next year.

11. Oscar Henwood

Gippsland Power/Vic Country

MID, 185cm

Henwood was a key contributor in the Power's Talent League flag and plays with great composure. He can try to bite off too much with his time in possession but is typically creative and uses it really well in space.

12. Harvey Chapman

Sturt/South Australia

DEF, 195cm

Chapman is the lone key defender inside the top bracket of the draft 12 months out, though he plays a more natural role as a rebounder. The SA tall is an excellent kick and sets up play from the last line of defence with instructive ball use. He can intercept with his reading of the play and gets involved in attack up the field.

13. Sam Husband (Tasmania Academy)

Tasmania Devils/Allies

MID, 180cm

The Devils didn't pre-list Husband because they have priority access to Tasmanian in the draft. He's the premier Tassie prospect in their inaugural draft and will be the poster boy of local talent for the 19th team. He's already played two seasons of Talent League football and is at his best using his evasiveness and skills around stoppages.

14. Campbell Creyk

West Perth/Western Australia

MID, 182cm

Creyk surged into the first round mix this year as a contested beast through the midfield. He rips the ball out of stoppages and doesn't often lose one-on-ones, playing with a hard edge that will serve him well at the next level. He will need to round out his game on the outside to continue pushing up draft boards.

15. Taj Garrett

Sturt/South Australia

MID, 183cm

A hard-running midfielder, Garrett's thirst to find the ball and work to contests is an important facet of his game. He outworks opponents and gets forward of the ball to impact. He may play his best football off a wing in the AFL but will get ample exposure on-ball for Sturt next year.

stories.headline: Revisiting sports and pop culture from GTA V's launch
stories.summary: "Grand Theft Auto VI" was released Thursday following a 13-year wait since GTA V.
stories.body:
Peyton Manning was beginning a record-setting season. Joel Embiid had yet to play a college basketball game. And "Breaking Bad" hadn't reached its finale.

That was 4,812 days ago, when "Grand Theft Auto V" arrived on Sept. 17, 2013.

More than 13 years later, "Grand Theft Auto VI" launches Thursday, with athletes and teams counting down to its release -- and looking back at how much has changed.

Houston Rockets center Steven Adams even quipped during media day that performances could be impacted by the game's release.

"So look at NFL, look at all the leagues and watch them plummet. Just for the month of November, performances are going to go down," Adams said.

Before finding out whether Adams' prediction holds up, here's a look at the sports and pop culture landscape when GTA V arrived -- Sept. 17, 2013.

Seattle and Denver were starting their Super Bowl runs

The NFL had just finished its second week and two squads were in the early stages of dominant campaigns: Seattle and Denver.

The Seahawks' defense proved to be its superpower, earning the "Legion of Boom" nickname. Seattle allowed 273.6 yards and 14.4 points per game, both the fewest in the regular season. The Broncos averaged a league-high 457.3 yards and 37.9 points per game, while Peyton Manning tossed an NFL record 5,477 yards plus 55 touchdowns.

Both teams would finish with 13-3 records, setting up a Super Bowl meeting in February 2014. Seattle would emerge victorious on the biggest stage after stifling Denver's offense in a 43-8 victory -- and the seeds of Super Bowl XLVIII were sprouting as GTA V was released.

Miami Heat looking to three-peat

The LeBron James, Dwyane Wade and Chris Bosh Big Three were entering their fourth season as teammates following back-to-back titles.

Miami edged out the San Antonio Spurs in the 2013 NBA Finals, an instant classic. The Heat faced a series clinching defeat in Game 6 before Ray Allen's late 3-pointer sent it into overtime. The extra period ended in a Miami victory to force a Game 7, where it closed out another championship.

The Heat faced the Spurs in a rematch in 2014, and San Antonio got its revenge this time around. But, for two straight summers, Miami reigned supreme.

Five stars preparing to go one-and-done

The 2013 college basketball freshman class had its fair share of heavy hitters.

In March 2013, then-high schoolers Andrew Wiggins and Jabari Parker graced the cover of Slam Magazine with the headline "Young Money: The game's next superstars have arrived." Wiggins and Parker were No. 1 and 2, respectively, in the SC Next rankings, but they were far from the only top prospects.

Joel Embiid, Julius Randle and Aaron Gordon all featured in the top 10 of the rankings as five-star prospects. Each of them, alongside Wiggins and Parker, went one-and-done and were selected in the top 10 of the 2014 NBA draft. Other notable names in the 2013 high school class included twins Aaron and Andrew Harrison, Noah Vonleh and Wayne Selden.

'Breaking Bad' nears its end as 'Roar' rules the charts

One of the greatest TV shows of all time, the final season of "Breaking Bad" aired as GTA V came out.

Two days before its release, the iconic "Ozymandias" episode aired. Series creator Vince Gilligan said that the episode is the "best episode we ever have had or ever will have." It remains one of the highest-rated episodes of the series on IMDB with 9.5 stars.

Pop songs led the way on the Billboard Hot 100 the week GTA V came out. Katy Perry's "Roar" hit No. 1 on Sept. 16, 2013, at the time matching Rihanna for the most No. 1's in the chart's 21-year history at 10. It took six weeks for "Roar" to reach No. 1, then-the fastest No. 1 hit since Perry's "California Gurls" in 2010.

Slotted in at No. 2 was "Blurred Lines" by Robin Thicke featuring T.I. and Pharrell. That track spent 10 weeks on the top before being dethroned. Lorde's "Royals" was at No. 3, while Jay-Z and Justin Timberlake's "Holy Grail" sat at No. 4.

The rest of the songs on the charts' top 10 included: "Wake Me Up!" by Avicii, "Summertime Sadness" by Lana Del Rey vs. Cedric Gervais, "Applause" by Lady Gaga, "Hold On, We're Going Home" by Drake featuring Majid Jordan, "Safe And Sound" by Capital Cities and "Berzerk" by Eminem.

WNBA, MLB teams were building championship legacies

The Minnesota Lynx won their second WNBA championship in 2013, and it would mark the beginning of a dynasty. Minnesota won two more in 2015 and 2017, the latter of which made it four titles in seven seasons as the club also won in 2011. Hall of Famer Maya Moore played a key role in each of the four championships. In 2013, she averaged 20.9 points on 53% shooting in the playoffs.

MLB saw similar dominance in alternating years from the San Francisco Giants. San Francisco missed the postseason in 2013 after World Series titles in 2010 and 2012. Someone privy to a trend could've predicted that the Giants would win it again in 2014 -- which they did. San Francisco hasn't won a World Series since, however.

BCS era coming to a close

College athletics looked entirely different 13 years ago, to say the least.

One of the biggest changes in college football lies in the implementation of the playoff system. Previously, the sport used the BCS rankings for 16 years to determine which two teams would play in the national championship game. That system had its fair share of controversies and came to a close following the 2013 campaign.

Florida State and Auburn made sure the BCS era went out with a bang at the Rose Bowl. Facing a four-point deficit with 1:05 left, Heisman-winning quarterback Jameis Winston led the Seminoles down the field for a game-winning touchdown. Two plays later Florida State closed it out to win 34-31 and clinch its first national championship since 1999 in memorable fashion.

stories.headline: First-half romp powers Jillaroos' fourth-straight Rugby League World Cup salute
stories.summary: Australia's Jillaroos have blown away New Zealand 34-10 to win a fourth-straight Women's Rugby League World Cup.
stories.body:
Australia have underlined their women's rugby league dominance with a 34-10 annihilation of New Zealand in the World Cup final.

The Jillaroos did the damage with six first-half tries on Sunday at Suncorp Stadium, with winger Jaime Chapman recording a brilliant hat-trick before the break to cap a historic tournament.

It was Australia's fourth straight Cup triumph, following a 54-4 win in the final four years ago and coming after New Zealand won the first three tournaments between 2000-08.

Chapman carried two players more than 10 metres to score her first, before flying into the corner for another and then busting through four tacklers for a sensational 70-metre solo effort.

Her treble gave her the equal record for tries in a World Cup -- for men or women -- at 13, matching the Kiwi Ferns' Honey Hireme-Smiler from 2017.

It seemed inevitable that she would go clear in the second half.

But both teams struggled in the Brisbane humidity, with the Kiwi Ferns' try in the finals seconds the only points of an error-riddled second period.

For the Jillaroos there were several poignant narratives to come out of the win.

Coach Jess Skinner's controversial decision to play five-eighth Jesse Southwell and drop Jocelyn Kelleher paid dividends.

Southwell schemed with the ball, landed five goals and was the perfect foil for half Tarryn Aiken, who controlled play with confidence and skill.

Chapman played in the pool games and semi-final in the 2022 World Cup but has now put an indelible stamp on a final.

"There is no better win than winning the World Cup on home turf," she told Channel Seven.

"We connected the first day we came into camp."

Fullback Tamika Upton sat out the tournament four years ago with a calf injury but now the five-time premiership winner has every team accolade in the game to her credit.

Prop Millie Elliott retires with a fairytale ending while dual international Sariah Paki, who was chased by the Ferns to play for them, has now won the World Cup in two sports after triumphing with the Australian rugby sevens side in 2022.

All the talk before the clash was the danger posed by New Zealand's Golden Boot winner and strike centre Stacey Waaka.

The former rugby union star, who had scored nine tries in the tournament, was snuffed out by Jillaroos captain Isabelle Kelly, who confronted Waaka all match and gave her no space.

As the Jillaroos' big guns stood up, centre Jessica Sergis scored her 23rd try in 18 Tests with a 70m dash through the middle off an undetected forward pass.

Aiken turned second-rower Shaylee Bent inside for the second try of the match while Upton started and finished a movement that had her attacking fingerprints all over it.

Ferns fullback Apii Nicholls was her side's best player in a dynamic display until she tore a hamstring in the 66th minute.
